Jabir's father, martyred at Uhud, left heavy debts; the Prophet sat on the biggest date heap and measured out until all were paid, the heaps still seeming whole.
Jihad follows timely prayer and kindness to parents, no deed equals it, women's best jihad is Hajj, and the Prophet dreams of followers fighting at sea, Umm Haram among them.
Paradise has a hundred grades for fighters and a house of martyrs; a morning or evening in Allah's cause outweighs the world, and martyrs wish to be killed again.
But for men he cannot mount, the Prophet would join every army unit, and he wishes repeated martyrdom; he announces Zaid, Ja'far and Ibn Rawaha martyred, and Khalid victorious.
The Prophet dreamt of followers sailing the sea like kings on thrones, Umm Haram among the first; she joined Mu'awiya's naval expedition and died falling from her mount on return.
Of seventy sent to Bani Amir, all but a lame man are killed after the envoy's stabbing; Gabriel says their Lord is pleased; the Prophet curses the killers forty days.
The Prophet tells his bleeding finger its wound is in Allah's cause; anyone wounded in His cause comes on Resurrection Day with a wound coloured like blood, scented like musk.
Heraclius tells Abu Sufyan that apostles are tested by battles of alternating success, but the final victory is always theirs.
Anas bin an-Nadr falls at Uhud with over eighty wounds, the verse on such men found with Khuzaima; a convert soon martyred is richly rewarded, and Haritha is in Firdaus.
Whoever fights so that Allah's word is highest fights in His cause, and one whose feet are covered with dust in His cause will not be touched by the Fire.
While building the mosque the Prophet wipes dust from Ammar, who carries two bricks at a time, saying a rebellious group will kill him as he calls them to Allah.
Returning from the Trench, the Prophet has bathed when Gabriel, dust on his head, says he has not put down arms and points him toward Bani Quraiza.
The Prophet curses Bir Mauna's killers thirty days; some who drank alcohol that morning are martyred at Uhud; angels shade Jabir's slain father; Paradise is under the shades of swords.
Solomon swore a hundred women would each bear a knight for Allah's cause but did not say 'Allah willing', so only one bore a half-man; had he, all would have.
The Prophet, best, bravest and most generous, rides out ahead when Medina takes fright, and, mobbed by bedouins after Hunain, says they will find him no miser, liar or coward.
Sa'd teaches his sons the Prophet's refuge after prayer from cowardice, decrepit old age, worldly trials and the grave's punishment; the Prophet also sought refuge from helplessness and laziness.
As-Sa'ib heard none of Talha, Sa'd, al-Miqdad and Abdur-Rahman bin Auf narrate from the Prophet, except Talha, who talked about the day of Uhud.
On the day of the Conquest the Prophet says there is no emigration after it, only jihad and intention, and those called to fight must go forth at once.
Allah smiles at a martyr and his killer, later forgiven and martyred, both entering Paradise; at Khaibar a son of Sa'id says Allah honoured through him a Muslim he killed.
Abu Talha did not fast in the Prophet's lifetime because of jihad, but after his death was never seen without fasting except on the two Eids.
Five are martyrs: those who die of plague, abdominal disease, drowning, or a falling building, and those killed in Allah's cause; plague is martyrdom for every Muslim.
When the verse ranking those who strive above those who sit at home came, the blind Ibn Umm Maktum complained, and revelation added the exception for the disabled.
Abdullah bin Abi Aufa wrote that the Prophet said to be patient when facing the enemy.
Digging the trench, cold and hungry Emigrants and Ansar pledge lifelong jihad, while the Prophet, carrying earth, asks Allah to forgive and bless them and grant calm and firm feet.
Anas recalls returning from Tabuk, and on a campaign the Prophet said those held back in Medina by an excuse share the reward of every pass and valley crossed.
Fasting one day for Allah's pleasure keeps one's face seventy years from the Fire, and whoever spends two things in His cause is called by all Paradise's gatekeepers.

The Prophet fears only worldly blessings: wealth is sweet vegetation, excellent when lawfully gained and spent on Allah's cause, orphans, the poor and travellers; the unlawful taker is never satisfied.
Equipping a fighter or caring well for his family earns a fighter's reward, and the Prophet visits Umm Sulaim out of pity, her brother having been killed with him.
At Yamama Thabit bin Qais, perfuming himself with hunut, takes his place and refuses to flee; on the day of the Clans az-Zubair volunteers to scout, called the Prophet's disciple.
Leaving the Prophet, Malik bin al-Huwairith and a friend are told to give the adhan and iqama themselves and let the elder lead the prayer.
Good remains in horses' foreheads till Resurrection, bringing reward or booty; a horse kept for Allah's cause earns reward for its feed and dung; horses named al-Jarada and al-Luhaif appear.
Mu'adh, riding behind the Prophet on the donkey Ufair, learns that Allah's right is to be worshipped alone, and that He will not punish those who worship none besides Him.
When Medina took fright, the Prophet borrowed a horse called Mandub, rode out, found nothing to fear, and said the horse was very fast.
The Prophet said evil omen is in three things, the horse, the woman and the house, or, in another wording, if it is in anything it is in these.
Horses bring reward, shelter or sin; the Prophet speeds Jabir's tired camel and buys it, finds Mandub fast, and gives a horse two booty shares, its rider one.
Al-Bara says the Prophet did not flee at Hunain when Hawazin's archers turned on Muslims collecting booty, but stayed on his white mule declaring himself the Prophet in truth.
As his foot entered the stirrup and his she-camel rose with him, the Prophet began the Talbiya at the mosque of Dhul-Hulaifa.
The Prophet rode an unsaddled horse, sword slung on, Abu Talha's slow horse became unbeatable, he arranged horse races over set courses, and his she-camel al-Adba was once outrun.
Al-Bara says the Prophet did not flee at Hunain; the hasty fled when Hawazin shot at them, while he rode his white mule declaring he was the Prophet in truth.
Women's jihad is Hajj; Umm Haram asks to join the sea fighters; the Prophet draws lots among his wives; women carry water, treat the wounded, bring back the dead.
